topic: Property Law: Specific Transfers (Sale, Mortgage, Lease, Gift)
description: This module delves into the specific modes of transferring property under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. It breaks down the legal definitions, essential elements, and operational rules for Sales, Mortgages (including the right of redemption), Leases, and Gifts.

key_points: Definition: 'Sale' is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised.

Essential Elements: There must be two competent parties (seller and buyer), the subject matter must be transferable immovable property, and there must be 'consideration' in the form of money (price). If the exchange is for another property, it is an 'Exchange', not a sale.

Registration: For tangible immovable property of the value of Rs. 100 and upwards, the transfer can be made ONLY by a registered instrument. Delivery of possession alone is not sufficient to transfer legal title in such cases.

Definition: A mortgage is the transfer of an 'interest' in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced (a loan). The transferor is the mortgagor, and the transferee is the mortgagee.

Types of Mortgages: The TPA recognizes six types, including Simple Mortgage (no delivery of possession, personal liability to pay), Mortgage by Conditional Sale, Usufructuary Mortgage (possession given, rent/profits adjust the interest/principal), English Mortgage, Mortgage by deposit of title deeds (Equitable mortgage), and Anomalous Mortgage.

Right of Redemption (Section 60): This is the most crucial right of the mortgagor. Once the principal and interest are paid, the mortgagor has an absolute right to get back the property. The legal maxim is 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. Any condition in the mortgage deed that prevents redemption is a 'clog on redemption' and is legally void.

Lease: It is a transfer of a 'right to enjoy' immovable property for a certain time, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid (premium) or periodic money/service (rent). It transfers possession, not ownership. It differs from a 'License' (which grants mere permission to do something on the land without transferring any interest).
Gift: A transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and 'without consideration'.

Acceptance of Gift: The gift must be accepted by or on behalf of the donee during the lifetime of the donor and while the donor is still capable of giving. If the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void.

Registration of Gift: A gift of immovable property MUST be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses, regardless of the property's value.

questions.question: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, how must a sale of tangible immovable property worth Rs. 500,000 be legally executed?

options.A: Merely by physical delivery of possession to the buyer.
options.B: Through an oral agreement in front of the village head (Sarpanch).
options.C: Only by a registered written instrument (sale deed).
options.D: By signing a temporary MoU and paying a token amount.

questions.explanation: Section 54 of the TPA mandates that the sale of tangible immovable property of the value of Rs. 100 and upwards can be made ONLY by a registered instrument. Delivery of possession or oral agreements hold no legal validity for transferring ownership in such cases.

questions.question: An elderly woman executes a registered gift deed for her house in favor of her nephew out of love and affection. However, before the nephew can legally accept the gift, he tragically dies in a car accident. What happens to the gift?

options.A: The gift remains valid and the house transfers to the nephew's legal heirs.
options.B: The gift is void because acceptance must happen during the lifetime of both the donor and the donee.
options.C: The gift is valid because the deed was already registered by the donor.
options.D: The state government takes over the property.

questions.explanation: Under Section 122 of the TPA, a gift must be accepted by the donee during the lifetime of the donor. The section explicitly states that if the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void.

questions.question: Ramesh takes a loan of Rs. 10 Lakhs from a bank and mortgages his land. The mortgage deed contains a clause stating: 'If the loan is not repaid within 5 years, the right to redeem the property shall be permanently extinguished, and the bank will become the absolute owner.' After 6 years, Ramesh arranges the money and wants to repay the loan to get his land back. Can he do so?

options.A: No, because he signed the contract and is bound by the 5-year limit.
options.B: No, because ownership automatically transferred to the bank on the 5th anniversary.
options.C: Yes, because the clause is a 'clog on the equity of redemption' and is completely void; his right to redeem survives.
options.D: Yes, but he must pay double the interest as a penalty for crossing the deadline.

questions.explanation: This is a classic example of a 'clog on redemption'. The right of redemption (Section 60) is absolute and cannot be contracted away. Courts consider any clause that penalizes or prevents the mortgagor from getting their property back after repaying the debt as void. 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage.'
